title: The Case for Plant-Forward Food Systems in Addressing Child Undernutrition in Latin America: Lessons from Ecuador
abstract: Child undernutrition remains a major public health challenge in Latin America, as in other low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Responses range from micronutrient supplementation to novel food products. Fish-based “blue food” gummies developed in Ecuador to deliver iron and zinc to children in fishing communities are one recent example of product-centered approaches that use animal-source foods. This perspective focuses on Latin America, using Ecuador as its anchoring case, and draws on evidence from other LMICs to inform the regional context. This perspective does not argue against animal-source foods in general. It critiques product-centered nutrition interventions (formulated or reformulated commodities designed mainly to deliver micronutrients) and uses Ecuador’s fish-based gummies as an illustrative case. We define plant-forward food systems as approaches that prioritize diverse, culturally embedded plant foods as dietary foundations, with animal-source foods as complementary when contextually warranted. This framing builds on demonstrated food-systems programs, including biofortification and vegetable-system initiatives, rather than treating plant-forward strategies as merely prospective alternatives. Legumes, whole grains, tubers, seeds, and traditional crops, abundant throughout Latin America, offer substantial nutritional potential when appropriately combined, prepared, and, where necessary, fortified. When well designed and adapted to local contexts, plant-forward strategies can address micronutrient adequacy, dietary habit formation, food sovereignty, climate resilience, and long-term affordability together. We argue for rebalancing nutrition policy in Latin America toward food-systems approaches that place plants at the dietary foundation, with animal-source foods as contextually appropriate complements rather than primary solutions.
